title: My Lagan Love
description: Belfast poet Joseph Campbell wrote the words and Belfast-born composer Herbert Hughes published the air in 1904, a lament for a girl by the River Lagan. Kate Bush recorded it in 1989; the river meets the city at Lagan Weir.

title: Softly, Softly
description: Ruby Murray, raised off the Donegall Road in south Belfast, took this ballad to No. 1 in Britain in 1955 and once had five singles in the Top 20 in the same week. Belfast unveiled a blue plaque to her in 2019.

title: Gloria
description: Them, the band fronted by a teenage Van Morrison, built this three-chord stomp in their residency at the Maritime Hotel’s R&B club. Countless garage bands copied it; the old seamen’s hotel on College Square North is long gone.

title: Cyprus Avenue
description: Van Morrison, born a mile away on Hyndford Street, turned this leafy, well-off east Belfast avenue into the centrepiece of his 1968 album Astral Weeks. In 2015 he played a 70th-birthday concert on the street itself.

title: Belfast Boy
description: English singer Don Fardon’s tribute to footballer George Best, the Manchester United winger who grew up on the Cregagh council estate in east Belfast. Best’s boyhood home on Burren Way is still visited by fans.

title: Stairway to Heaven
description: Led Zeppelin, the London rock band, played this song live for the first time at the Ulster Hall on 5 March 1971, months before it came out on record. The Victorian concert hall on Bedford Street still hosts gigs.

title: Big Time
place: Good Vibrations record shop, Great Victoria Street
description: Belfast punks Rudi made this the first single on Good Vibrations, the label run by record-shop owner Terri Hooley from Great Victoria Street. His shop gave young fans a scene across the sectarian divide during the Troubles.

title: Alternative Ulster
description: Stiff Little Fingers, from Belfast, shouted about life under the Troubles, the decades of conflict over Northern Ireland’s future, with soldiers on every corner. Punks crowded the Harp Bar on Hill Street to hear bands like them.

title: Annie’s Song
description: Flautist James Galway, who grew up in working-class north Belfast and learned in local flute bands, took this instrumental of John Denver’s love song to No. 3 in Britain. The pin is the York Road, spine of his old district.

title: I’ll Tell Me Ma
description: A children’s skipping song whose chorus crowns “the belle of Belfast city”; Van Morrison recorded it with Irish folk group the Chieftains on Irish Heartbeat. Belfast City Hall, the domed civic heart of the city, stands for her.

title: Glue
description: Belfast DJ duo Bicep wrote this wistful track out of nostalgia for 1990s rave. Shine, the long-running club night at Queen’s University Students’ Union, anchored the Belfast dance scene they grew up in.

title: C.E.A.R.T.A.
place: Cultúrlann McAdam Ó Fiaich, Falls Road
description: The title means “rights.” West Belfast rap trio Kneecap rhyme in Irish and English about a member refusing to speak English to police. Their Irish-language scene centres on Cultúrlann, an arts centre on the Falls Road.
